scope: GuitarHub guitar preparation, D/A chord, change, study, timing, and original single-string riff instruction: twenty-one authored lessons.

instructionConventions.handNames: Use picking hand and fretting hand; mirror physical diagrams for the selected handedness while retaining string numbers and note identities.
instructionConventions.stringNumbers: String 6 is the thick low E; string 1 is the thin high E.
instructionConventions.fretNumbers: Open is 0. Fret 1 is the space between the nut and first metal fret; place a fretting fingertip close to the metal fret on the body side of that space, not on top of it.
instructionConventions.practiceTiming: Segment durations are suggested attention blocks that sum to the existing lesson duration. They are not countdown deadlines for competence. Pause or repeat as needed.
instructionConventions.evidence: Reading responses, listening judgments, comfort checks, and technique checks are self-assessed unless a specific implemented measurement is identified. A monophonic pitch estimate does not prove chord correctness, buzzing, posture, or timing.
instructionConventions.referenceAudio: Reference sounds demonstrate target pitch, not realistic guitar timbre. Stop reference playback before listening for the learner's input; synthesized audio must not score its own exercise.

support-and-pick.description: Original seated silhouette showing guitar body on thigh, body lightly against torso, picking forearm resting over the body edge, and a relaxed fretting hand that does not carry the instrument. Include an inset of thumb pad meeting the side of a gently curled index finger around a pick, with only its tip exposed.
support-and-pick.textAlternative: Support the guitar with your body and forearm so the fretting hand is free to move. Hold the pick between thumb and index finger with a small tip showing.

six-open-strings.playback: User-triggered single-string reference, 1.5 seconds long with a soft attack and release; label the string, note, and octave. Wait for it to stop before the learner plucks. Also offer an unscored low-to-high sequence.

flat-target-sharp.description: Play the target then one comparison tone with a short silent gap. These deliberately separated examples teach direction; 50 cents is not a tuning pass threshold.

tuner-directions.description: A selected A2 target with textual states Below target, In tune, and Above target. Show the selected string number and octave next to the reading. Do not hard-code a clockwise peg direction because headstock layouts differ.

notation-legend.description: Three separate original panels: horizontal tab with high E at top and low E at bottom; an upright chord diagram labeled with string numbers, nut, frets, X and O; a 4/4 bar with four quarter-note rhythm slashes aligned to beat numbers 1–4. lessons.title: Three Points of Contact
lessons.objective: Support the guitar without gripping the neck and make a small, controlled picking motion.

steps.title: Let the guitar rest
steps.action: Sit on a steady armless chair with feet supported. Rest the body on a thigh, keep it lightly against your torso, and rest your picking forearm over the body. Raise the neck a little if that makes reaching easier.
steps.lookCheck: The guitar stays in place when you briefly relax your fretting hand. Your shoulders stay low.
steps.listenCheck: No sound is required for this step.

steps.title: Free the fretting hand
steps.action: Bring your fretting hand around the neck with the thumb resting lightly behind it. Bend the fingertips toward the strings without squeezing. Relax and repeat.
steps.lookCheck: You can move your fingers while the guitar remains supported; avoid forcing your wrist into a deep bend.
steps.listenCheck: Keep your hand relaxed; no note is needed yet.

steps.title: Make a small pick stroke
steps.action: Hold a pick between your thumb and the side of a gently curled index finger. Leave a small tip showing. Touch the thin first string and move the pick just far enough through it to release the string, then stop.
steps.lookCheck: The stroke crosses one string instead of sweeping across its neighbors.
steps.listenCheck: Hear one attack. Tuning happens next, so do not judge its pitch yet.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The neck drops when the fretting hand relaxes.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Adjust the body support or use a strap so that hand is not holding up the guitar.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The pick catches or several strings sound.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use a smaller motion and less exposed pick; start with the pick already touching the intended string.

practiceSegments.instruction: Set the guitar down, pick it up, and find a supported position twice.
Relax the fretting hand, then return it to the neck five times without shifting the guitar.
Make six gentle strokes on the thin first string, leaving silence between them.
Release both hands, settle your shoulders, and choose one setup adjustment to keep.

criteria: I can let go with my fretting hand while keeping the guitar supported.
I can touch and pick one intended string.
I can relax my grip between strokes.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can repeat the setup and controlled stroke without forcing the position.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repeat only the support or pick step that needs attention; stop and adjust if the position hurts.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own check of the starting setup and a controlled pick stroke.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Tuning, tone quality, or comfort during longer playing sessions.

lessons.title: Six Open Strings
lessons.objective: Connect each string number and name with one deliberately picked open-string note.

steps.title: Find before playing
steps.action: Confirm tuning first. Point to strings 6 through 1 and say Low E, A, D, G, B, High E. Leave your fretting fingers clear of the strings.
steps.lookCheck: The selected label points to the actual string, including which E it means.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to an optional reference only before your own note.

steps.title: Sound one target
steps.action: Pluck the requested string once with a small stroke. Let it settle and ring; do not keep striking while waiting for pitch feedback.
steps.lookCheck: The pick touches the requested string and the next string stays still.
steps.listenCheck: Hear one sustained note rather than two strings together.

steps.title: Reset between notes
steps.action: Touch the ringing string lightly to stop it, then move to the next requested string. If the result is uncertain, let the room go quiet and make one fresh attempt.
steps.lookCheck: Check the next string name before moving.
steps.listenCheck: There is a short quiet gap between target notes.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Mute the strings, place the pick against the target, and make a smaller stroke.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The pitch display jumps or does not settle.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop other sounds and reference playback, check tuning and microphone access, then pluck once. Use your ears to check for extra ringing or buzz.

practiceSegments.instruction: Check tuning and identify all six strings without playing.
Play 6–5–4–3–2–1 slowly, muting between notes; repeat if time allows.
Choose the two strings you confused most and alternate between them with a quiet reset.
Make a fresh low-to-high pass and note which string still needs review.

criteria: I can distinguish low E from high E.
I choose the named string before picking.
I can stop one note before starting the next.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can complete the sequence at your own pace with deliberate string choices; replay any uncertain target.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to tuning if the target pitch remains wrong; repeat just the confused string pair otherwise.
selfAssessment.proves: Any available pitch feedback for the single notes in this attempt.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Steady tempo, fretting accuracy, fret buzz, or chord quality.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Six Open Strings
lessons.objective: Check whether you can find the strings independently and hear when more than one sounds.

steps.title: Prepare a quiet check
steps.action: Check tuning and stop any reference tones. Keep the string-name diagram available for preparation, then hide it for your first pass.
steps.lookCheck: Check whether you are using microphone feedback or your own listening check.
steps.listenCheck: Only the guitar should supply the attempted note.

steps.title: Make one complete pass
steps.action: Say each string name, then pluck strings 6 through 1 once each. Mute between notes. Use as much time as needed; this is not a rhythm race.
steps.lookCheck: Compare the selected string with your intended string.
steps.listenCheck: Notice any extra ringing string or unclear attack yourself.

steps.title: Use the result
steps.action: Repeat the least certain string after checking its label. Finish with one more complete pass and record one improvement or one item to revisit.
steps.lookCheck: Keep this attempt separate from earlier practice results.
steps.listenCheck: Judge extra ringing by ear; do not treat a pitch match as proof of clean tone.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You reach for a string by habit without checking its name.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Pause, point to the requested string, say its name, and then play.

mistakeRecovery.observation: No reliable microphone result is available.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use your own listening check and save what you noticed. A self-check does not give a microphone pitch score.

practiceSegments.instruction: Complete the first independent six-string pass.
Review the least certain string with the diagram.
Repeat the complete pass and record your self-check.

criteria: I named each string before playing it.
I controlled the start and stop of each note.
I know which string, if any, needs another check.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can find all six strings without guessing and can repeat an uncertain note deliberately.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Revisit the open-string exercise for the strings you confused; you can continue practicing reading too.
selfAssessment.proves: Your string choices and listening check, plus any available pitch feedback.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Clean fretted notes, chord competence, or rhythmic accuracy.

lessons.title: What In Tune Actually Means
lessons.objective: Understand a tuning target and identify whether a note is below or above it.

steps.title: Name the target
steps.action: Select string 5, A2, and point to it on the guitar. Listen once to the reference. A note name alone is not enough: the two E strings share a letter but have different pitches.
steps.lookCheck: The target shows both the string and octave.
steps.listenCheck: Compare the low and high E references; the high E is clearly higher.

steps.title: Hear the direction
steps.action: Listen to the A2 target, then the lower example, then target again. Repeat with the higher example and name which direction changed.
steps.lookCheck: Read Below target and Above target rather than relying on color.
steps.listenCheck: Compare height of pitch, not loudness or guitar-like tone.

steps.title: Read a small difference
steps.action: View the tuner diagram. Flat means below the selected target; sharp means above it. Cents describe small pitch differences, with 100 cents between adjacent semitones. Your first task is direction and a settled reading, not speed.
steps.lookCheck: A stable in-tune indication belongs to the correct selected string and octave.
steps.listenCheck: One cleanly picked string is easier to compare than several ringing together.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You match the letter E but not which E.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Check string 6/E2 versus string 1/E4 before touching a tuning peg.
Replay references at the same volume and focus only on pitch height.

practiceSegments.instruction: Identify the six named targets and compare the two E references.
Compare the target with lower and higher examples; say the direction before revealing its label.
Read the three textual tuner states and point to the next action each implies.
Explain the difference between a correct note letter and a correct string/octave.

criteria: I know flat means lower and sharp means higher than the selected target.
I check which string and octave I am tuning.
I know to play one string at a time.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can choose the target and explain the tuning direction; fine ear matching can develop with practice.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Replay the lower/target/higher examples and use the visual tuner alongside your ears.
selfAssessment.proves: Understanding of tuner labels and targets.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: An in-tune instrument or trained pitch discrimination.

lessons.title: Tuner Target Practice
lessons.objective: Make small tuning corrections while keeping the selected string and octave correct.

steps.title: Connect string to peg
steps.action: Start with string 6, low E2. Follow that string visually from the nut to its tuning machine before adjusting anything. Select the same target in the tuner and pluck it gently.
steps.lookCheck: The target, played string, and touched peg all agree.
steps.listenCheck: Mute other strings and wait for one note to settle.

steps.title: Correct a little
steps.action: If below target, increase tension a small amount; if above, lower it a little, then approach the target with a small upward adjustment. Repluck after each change. Do not deliberately detune the whole guitar for this exercise.
steps.lookCheck: Confirm that the reading moves toward the intended target; peg rotation differs by guitar.
steps.listenCheck: The pitch changes smoothly in the intended direction. If unsure which octave or peg is correct, stop and recheck before tightening further.

steps.title: Work across and recheck
steps.action: Repeat for A2, D3, G3, B3, and E4. Return to low E and check all six again; changing one string can slightly alter others.
steps.lookCheck: Each reading is settled on its named target, not a brief flash while the note attacks.
steps.listenCheck: Let each note stop before checking the next.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The display follows the wrong string or jumps between notes.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Mute everything, verify the string/peg path, and pick only the selected string after reference audio stops.
Use much smaller adjustments and pause to repluck. Treat an already tuned string as a successful check; it does not need to be detuned.

practiceSegments.instruction: Prepare the tuner and verify the low-E peg.
Check and gently adjust the six strings. Pause the lesson timer if more time is needed.
Recheck the complete guitar, correcting only strings that need it.
Name one adjustment you made and how you knew its direction.

criteria: I verified each string's tuning peg before adjusting.
I made small changes toward the correct target.
I rechecked all six strings.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: All six strings have been checked against their correct targets using a working tuner.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Continue slowly. If the app reading is unreliable, use a trusted external tuner and note which tuner you used.
selfAssessment.proves: Your check of all six strings with a tuner.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Tuning by ear, tuning quickly, or perfect intonation at every fret. A checklist alone does not measure pitch.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Check All Six Strings
lessons.objective: Check and correct tuning independently, then verify the whole guitar again.

steps.title: Start where the guitar is
steps.action: Use the guitar's current tuning. Do not loosen all strings or create a large detuning. Prepare the tuner and name the six targets before the attempt.
steps.lookCheck: The checklist has one row per actual string, including separate low and high E.
steps.listenCheck: Stop all reference and backing sounds before your note.

steps.title: Check every string
steps.action: For each string, identify its peg, pluck, read the target, adjust only if necessary, and repluck to confirm. A string already in tune still earns a checked row.
steps.lookCheck: A stable correct target matters more than the elapsed time.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for one isolated note. Check any rattle or buzz by ear as well as reading its pitch.

steps.title: Confirm after adjustments
steps.action: Make a final six-string pass without skipping the strings you checked first. Save whether the check used app readings or your own external tuner.
steps.lookCheck: Confirm each string after checking it with the tuner.
steps.listenCheck: Compare any doubtful string again before moving to pitch practice.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You rush through the tuning check.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Take the time you need to check all six targets and make the final pass.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A string drifts after another adjustment.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Correct it slightly and repeat the final pass. This is why the recheck is part of tuning.

practiceSegments.instruction: Prepare and say the six target names.
Complete the six-string tuning check at a comfortable pace.
Make the final verification pass; extend the time if needed.
Record the check method and any unresolved string.

criteria: I checked all six named targets.
I verified the peg before each adjustment.
I completed a final pass after the last adjustment.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: The guitar is checked and any unresolved tuning problem is identified before pitch exercises.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to the target-practice steps or use an external tuner. Leave the tuning status incomplete if any string is unresolved.
selfAssessment.proves: Your completed six-string check and the tuner you used.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Tuning by ear or at speed. Confirming a checklist alone does not measure pitch.

lessons.title: Tab, Boxes, and Slashes
lessons.objective: Translate a simple tab number, chord-box symbol, and beat slash into the right action.

steps.title: Read a tab position
steps.action: Find the top tab line: it is thin string 1. The bottom is thick string 6. A number tells you the fret, not the finger. Point to 0 on the top line, then pluck open string 1.
steps.lookCheck: Match the labeled line to the guitar string before looking at the number.
steps.listenCheck: The 0 sounds the already learned open note.

steps.title: Read a chord box
steps.action: Use the upright diagram: vertical lines are strings and horizontal divisions are frets. O means play open; X means leave that string silent. Finger numbers use 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 little. Compare the labeled A and D examples before hiding either name.
steps.lookCheck: A starts on string 5; D starts on string 4. Trace each marked dot to its string and fret.
steps.listenCheck: Use the optional reference to hear the written pitches. Check the sound of your own chord by ear.

steps.title: Read time separately
steps.action: Look at four quarter-note slashes in the displayed 4/4 bar. Count 1, 2, 3, 4 while tapping your knee once per slash. The chord name tells what to hold; the rhythmic symbol tells when to play.
steps.lookCheck: Each slash sits on a numbered beat; keep reading left to right.
steps.listenCheck: Your taps follow the four reference clicks when the demo is used.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You read the bottom tab line as the thinnest string.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the string-number labels visible and point from the diagram to the instrument before playing.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You treat a tab 2 as finger 2 or strum an X string.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Name which notation you are reading, then consult its legend: tab numbers are frets; chord-box finger labels and X/O have separate jobs.

practiceSegments.instruction: Trace three tab prompts to the correct string and fret; play open-string prompts only.
Study the labeled A and D diagrams, identifying X, O, starting string, and each finger location.
Count and tap four displayed quarter-note slashes for four bars at a comfortable pace.
Explain in your own words what tab, a chord box, and rhythm slashes each tell you.

criteria: I know tab numbers show frets.
I can explain X and O.
I can identify a written beat separately from a chord shape.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can translate the demonstrated symbols into an action with the legend nearby.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repeat one notation panel at a time before mixing them.
selfAssessment.proves: Introductory reading comprehension.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Fluent sight-reading, chord execution, or measured rhythmic accuracy.

lessons.title: Name the Shape
lessons.objective: Recognize the introduced A and D diagrams and map their dots to your own fingers without a speed requirement.

steps.title: Study, then name
steps.action: Review the labeled A and D diagrams once. Hide the title, choose A or D, then reveal the answer. Read the lowest sounding string and X/O marks aloud too.
steps.lookCheck: Use the dot locations and starting string, not only color.
steps.listenCheck: You can answer the diagram questions with the microphone off.

steps.title: Place D deliberately
steps.action: Place index at string 3 fret 2, middle at string 1 fret 2, then ring at string 2 fret 3. Leave string 4 open and avoid 5 and 6. Release, then compare the two diagrams again.
steps.lookCheck: Each fingertip approaches its own string; keep the ring finger from lying across the thin first string.
steps.listenCheck: If a picked string sounds dull, lift and reposition the finger touching it, then listen again.

steps.title: Place A deliberately
steps.action: With the A diagram visible, put index finger at string 3 fret 2, middle at string 4 fret 2, then ring at string 2 fret 2. Leave strings 5 and 1 open; avoid string 6. Place one finger at a time, then release.
steps.lookCheck: Dots, finger numbers, and real string positions agree.
steps.listenCheck: If you choose to pick strings 5–1 individually, listen for each note to ring clearly.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You guess the chord name without reading the positions.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Reveal the label and name two visible differences between A and D before trying again.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The shape is difficult to hold or a neighbor is muted.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Release pressure, place one fingertip at a time closer to its fret, and shorten the hold. Reading can progress while physical chord practice continues later.

practiceSegments.instruction: Name six shuffled A/D diagram cards, checking each answer after choosing.
Place and release D slowly three times, resting between attempts.
Place and release A slowly three times; no timed chord changes.
Name two fresh cards and explain their open and avoided strings.

criteria: I can tell A and D diagrams apart without color.
I can trace each dot to a string and fret.
I know the lowest string to sound in each shape.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You identify both diagrams and can map the positions deliberately; fast changes and clean full chords are later practice goals.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to the labeled diagrams and practice only the confused symbol or finger location.
selfAssessment.proves: Your diagram answers and your own check of finger positions.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: An automatic chord check, fluent changes, or clear sound from every string.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Eight of Ten Reads
lessons.objective: Check ten reading decisions and identify the notation category that needs review.

steps.title: Answer before revealing
steps.action: Read each prompt and choose your answer once before showing the explanation. Work without the legend for the first attempt, but take as much thinking time as you need.
steps.lookCheck: The prompt clearly distinguishes tab, a chord diagram, or a rhythm bar.
steps.listenCheck: You may use the reference audio while learning; the quiz checks your reading.

steps.title: Map one answer physically
steps.action: For a string/fret prompt, point to that position on the guitar. For a beat prompt, count and tap. For a chord prompt, name the shape and its lowest sounding string without racing to fret it.
steps.lookCheck: Your intended physical action matches the selected answer.
steps.listenCheck: Check the sound of your physical examples yourself. The quiz score comes from your answers.

steps.title: Review the misses
steps.action: After all ten answers, revisit each missed category using the matching diagram. Try again as a new attempt; keep the first result visible separately.
steps.lookCheck: Read your correct answers out of ten and the categories to revisit.
steps.listenCheck: Eight correct answers show your reading progress; keep practicing the sounds and movements too.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You keep choosing answers until one is accepted.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Your first answer counts toward the score. Use the explanation to review, then try a new attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A score below eight feels like a reason to repeat everything.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Review only the missed categories, then take a fresh attempt. Leave the material available for reference.

practiceSegments.instruction: Prepare the first attempt with the legend hidden.
Answer ten prompts, pausing the timer whenever needed.
Review missed categories using their diagrams and one physical example.
Record the score and choose the next review item.

quiz.scoring: Earn one point for each question answered correctly on the first try. There are ten questions and no time bonus. Eight correct answers meets this checkpoint.

items.prompt: Which guitar string does the top line of this labeled tab represent?
items.explanation: Standard horizontal guitar tab places the highest-pitched string at the top.

items.prompt: A 0 is written on string 1. What do you do?
items.explanation: Zero means play without fretting that string.

items.prompt: A 2 is written on the B-string line. Which position does it name?
items.explanation: The line identifies the string; the number identifies the fret.

items.prompt: A 3 is written on the high-E line. Where do you point?
items.explanation: High E is string 1, and the tab number requests fret 3.

items.prompt: What does X above a string in a chord box mean?
items.explanation: X marks a string that should not sound in this shape.

items.prompt: What does O above a string mean?
options: Use your thumb to fret it
items.explanation: O identifies a sounding string without a fretted position.

items.prompt: Which introduced chord does this diagram show?
options: The diagram names a single fret
items.explanation: This A shape has fretted positions on strings 4, 3, and 2 at fret 2, with string 5 open.

items.prompt: Which introduced chord does this diagram show?
options: The diagram names a single string
items.explanation: This D shape has an open fourth string, two fret-2 positions, and the B-string position at fret 3.

items.prompt: This 4/4 bar contains one quarter-note slash on each numbered beat. How many strokes are written?
items.explanation: The displayed bar has four beats and one written stroke per beat.

items.prompt: What is the lowest sounding string in this D diagram?
items.explanation: Strings 6 and 5 are marked X; string 4 is the first sounding string.

criteria: I answered before revealing the explanation.
I can describe the action behind the symbols I answered correctly.
I know which category to revisit.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: At least eight first-attempt answers are correct; review the remaining categories while continuing to use notation in practice.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Review the specific missed notation panels, then begin a separate new attempt.
selfAssessment.proves: Performance on these ten reading prompts.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: General sight-reading, clean chords, timing, or the completion of a guitar grade.

lessons.title: D, Then A
lessons.objective: Place D and A in the taught finger order and identify the strings each chord should sound.

steps.title: Place D one finger at a time
steps.action: After checking tuning, put your index finger on string 3, fret 2; your middle finger on string 1, fret 2; then your ring finger on string 2, fret 3. Leave string 4 open. Start a light downstroke at string 4 and stop after string 1.
steps.lookCheck: The three fingertips match the D diagram. Strings 6 and 5 are marked X and stay outside the stroke.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to the four intended strings. This first sound is a starting point, not a test.

steps.title: Build A with the index first
steps.action: Release D. Put your index finger on string 3, fret 2; your middle finger on string 4, fret 2; then your ring finger on string 2, fret 2. Leave strings 5 and 1 open. Start the downstroke at string 5.
steps.lookCheck: Across fretted strings 4, 3, 2 the finger numbers are 2, 1, 3. String 6 stays silent.
steps.listenCheck: A sounds from five strings. If a string is unclear, keep the position visible and check it separately in the next exercise.

steps.title: Compare the shared position
steps.action: Place D again and point to your index. Its string and fret also belong to this A shape. For now, read the two diagrams and say the starting string before each gentle strum.
steps.lookCheck: Index is on string 3, fret 2 in both shapes; the other fingers occupy different places.
steps.listenCheck: With the microphone off, compare the optional chord references. Listen for those pitches when you play your own strings.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You form A with the index on string 4.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Follow this lesson's 2–1–3 fingering across strings 4–2 so the index can remain on string 3 during the later anchor exercise.

mistakeRecovery.observation: D contains a low booming note.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Start at string 4. Rehearse a small downstroke over only strings 4–1 before trying the whole chord again.

practiceSegments.instruction: Place D in index, middle, ring order; say which strings sound.
Place A in index, middle, ring order; compare its starting string with D.
Read both diagrams, identify the shared index position, and make one unhurried attempt at each.

criteria: I can point to every D finger position and its open fourth string.
I can point to every A finger position and identify strings 5 and 1 as open.
I know which low strings to avoid.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can use the diagrams to build both shapes deliberately; fluent switching comes later.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to one diagram and place only one finger at a time.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own comparison of the chord diagrams with your finger positions.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Clean sound from every string or fluent chord changes.

lessons.title: Check D, Then A
lessons.objective: Spend three minutes on each chord, using an individual-string check to make useful corrections.

steps.title: Give D its three minutes
steps.action: Start the D block after tuning. Place index, middle, then ring as shown. Strum strings 4–1 softly. Pick 4, 3, 2, 1 separately; if one is unclear, adjust the fingertip touching that string or its neighbor. Strum again.
steps.lookCheck: Keep each finger near the fret within its own space. Check that the ring finger does not lie against string 1.
steps.listenCheck: Compare the unclear note before and after your adjustment. Listen for any remaining buzz.

steps.title: Use the same check on A
steps.action: When ready, begin the three-minute A block. Place index on 3/2, middle on 4/2, ring on 2/2. Strum 5–1, pick each of those strings separately, adjust one cause, then strum again.
steps.lookCheck: String 6 is outside the stroke. Make space beneath the ring finger for the open first string.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for each intended string rather than repeatedly striking the whole shape and hoping it improves.

steps.title: Repeat without racing
steps.action: Release your fingers briefly between repetitions and rebuild in the same order. Pause the block whenever you need to reset. Stop at a useful observation even if the sound is still developing.
steps.lookCheck: Your hand can release its pressure and return without a forced wrist position.
steps.listenCheck: Record one string that improved or still needs attention. Keep listening as you work through the practice block.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A strum sounds unclear but you cannot locate the cause.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Pick the intended strings individually from the lowest sounding string upward. Work on the first unclear string before another complete strum.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You squeeze harder on every repetition.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Release, settle the guitar, and rebuild slowly. Use only enough pressure to sound the note; stop and reset if playing hurts.

practiceSegments.instruction: D accuracy: place, strum, check strings 4–1 individually, adjust, and strum again; repeat slowly.
A accuracy: place, strum, check strings 5–1 individually, adjust, and strum again; repeat slowly.

criteria: I used the complete check on D and A.
I identified a particular unclear string or confirmed each intended string by ear.
I can name the adjustment I tried and describe what I heard.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You understand the checking method and can use it on either shape; keep developing the sound as you continue.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repeat the affected chord's block with its diagram and one string at a time.
selfAssessment.proves: Your chord practice and the specific sound you checked.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: An automatic judgment of chord clarity or playing comfort.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Check Both Chords
lessons.objective: Recall D and A, then check their sounding strings and identify anything to revisit.

steps.title: Try the shapes from memory
steps.action: Tune first. Look away from the diagram and place D, then A, one at a time. Reveal the diagram after each attempt and compare the intended positions.
steps.lookCheck: Note which shape you remembered and when you needed the diagram.
steps.listenCheck: There is no microphone score in this check.

steps.title: Check the actual strings
steps.action: For D, strum then pick strings 4–1 individually. For A, use 5–1. Make a small correction if a note is unclear and strum again.
steps.lookCheck: Check the low starting string before you sound each chord.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for clear notes and unwanted strings. Note any sound you are unsure about.

steps.title: Choose the next useful action
steps.action: Record which shapes you recalled and one string to revisit. Continue to the silent anchor lesson when both shapes make sense; keep the accuracy exercise available.
steps.lookCheck: The record distinguishes recall from sound quality.
steps.listenCheck: Keep working on chord sound as you move on to changes and the study.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Look at the diagram, rebuild, then try again as a new recall attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You can place the shapes but one string stays unclear.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Log that string and revisit its accuracy block. Take time to listen after each adjustment.

practiceSegments.instruction: Tune and prepare a memory attempt.
Recall and check D, then compare with the diagram.
Recall and check A, then compare with the diagram.
Revisit one uncertain string or shape.
Record your recall and listening observations.

criteria: I tried recalling both shapes before checking the diagram.
I checked the intended strings of each shape.
I recorded any note or position that still needs attention.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Both shapes are familiar enough to begin slow anchor movement; continue the accuracy work where needed.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use the D or A accuracy block again, with the specific issue you recorded.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own shape-recall and individual-string check.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Fast chord changes or playing a complete song.

lessons.title: Keep One Finger in Place
lessons.objective: Move silently between D and A while the index keeps contact with string 3.

steps.title: Start with a light D shape
steps.action: Place D without strumming. Rest the fingertips on the strings; you do not need full playing pressure for this silent exercise.
steps.lookCheck: Index touches string 3 in fret 2, middle touches string 1 in fret 2, and ring touches string 2 in fret 3.
steps.listenCheck: Keep the strings silent. You can leave the microphone off.

steps.title: Keep the index in contact
steps.action: Lift middle and ring while leaving the index on string 3. Slide the index slightly back within fret 2 to make room. Put middle on string 4, fret 2 and ring on string 2, fret 2 to form A.
steps.lookCheck: The index never changes string or fret; it may move a little within the same fret space.
steps.listenCheck: Watch the contact and placement without strumming.

steps.title: Return to D slowly
steps.action: Lift middle and ring again. Let the index move back toward its D position within fret 2, then place middle on 1/2 and ring on 2/3. Continue D–A–D for the two-minute practice block, pausing as needed.
steps.lookCheck: The guitar stays supported while the other two fingers move independently of the index.
steps.listenCheck: Keep the movement quiet and check each finger position.

mistakeRecovery.observation: All three fingers leave the strings.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop at D. Lift only middle and ring once, return them, then attempt the move toward A.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The index presses rigidly or the hand tenses.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Reduce to light contact and slow the move. The index can slide a little within fret 2; it is a guide, not a clamp.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read the three positions and form a light D shape.
Silently alternate D and A with index contact; keep the movement deliberate.
Release and identify whether the index stayed on string 3.

criteria: I kept the index touching string 3 within fret 2.
I moved middle and ring into the correct A and D positions.
I completed this as silent, light-contact practice.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can repeat the slow movement and understand the shared contact point; speed develops in a separate exercise.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Repeat only the lift-and-return part before attempting the full change.
selfAssessment.proves: Your visual check of the anchor movement.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Chord sound or change speed; those have their own exercises.

lessons.title: Count Your One-Minute Changes
lessons.objective: Make and record two separate sixty-second A/D switching attempts, counting each completed move yourself.

steps.title: Set up one chord pair
steps.action: Tune first. Read the A and D diagrams and choose A as the starting shape. Form it before the timer begins; this setup shape is not a change. Keep the microphone off for this exercise.
steps.lookCheck: Check that A is selected as the starting chord and the timer is set for 60 seconds.
steps.listenCheck: One light strum after arriving at the next basic shape is enough; this block works on switching, while the accuracy block works on clean sound.

steps.title: Alternate for sixty seconds
steps.action: Start. Move A to D and count 1, then D to A and count 2. Continue alternating one completed move at a time. Do not add a count for a strum that repeats the same shape or an abandoned move. Stop counting when the full minute ends.
steps.lookCheck: Count a move when the basic finger positions are formed. An imperfect sound can still count; lifting the hand without forming the next shape cannot.
steps.listenCheck: Say your count or keep your own tally. GuitarHub does not listen and count these chord changes.

steps.title: Reset, then start at D
steps.action: Rest and record the first count before resetting. Form D, start a new full minute, and alternate D–A–D with the same convention. Keep the two results separate.
steps.lookCheck: The previous attempt stays visible and its count is not carried into the new timer.
steps.listenCheck: If either attempt is interrupted, save it as interrupted practice and restart a full minute when ready.

steps.title: Choose the difficult move
steps.action: Review the two counts and return to a slow anchor movement if needed. Work toward 30 changes in a complete minute as an early guide; 60 is a longer-term goal. Do not rush the next attempt just to beat a number.
steps.lookCheck: Compare counts only for complete one-minute attempts using the same counting rule.
steps.listenCheck: Return to the accuracy blocks to work on chord sound separately from your change count.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You counted the initial chord or both chords as one pair.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Starting A is zero, arriving at D is one, and returning to A is two. Use this counting rule for each new attempt.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The timer was paused, hidden, or interrupted.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Save the time you practiced as a partial attempt. Start a fresh full minute before comparing change counts; do not turn a short attempt into an estimated one-minute count.

practiceSegments.instruction: Prepare A, review how to count each completed move, and reset to zero.
One full A-first alternating A/D attempt.
Rest and record the first count.
One full D-first alternating D/A attempt.
Record both attempts and choose what to revisit.

criteria: I used one count per completed transition and excluded the setup shape.
I kept the two sixty-second attempts separate.
I labeled interruptions or partial counts instead of treating them as a full-minute result.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can count each completed move consistently for a full minute. Around 30 changes supports early progress; continue toward 60 over time.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use the silent anchor block and try a fresh minute later. Do not trade all shape accuracy or comfort for speed.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own count of completed changes during the recorded practice time.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: A microphone chord count, clean chord sound, or playing a song.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Your One-Minute Count
lessons.objective: Record a fresh, complete one-minute switching attempt and review your count and chord shapes.

steps.title: Recall and prepare
steps.action: Recall A and D before using the diagram. Choose the starting chord and form it before starting the timer. Reset the count to zero.
steps.lookCheck: Check your chosen starting chord before beginning your manual count.
steps.listenCheck: No microphone is needed.

steps.title: Make a fresh one-minute attempt
steps.action: Alternate between A and D for 60 active uninterrupted seconds. Count each completed move once. At the end enter the count you observed and whether the basic shapes stayed recognizable.
steps.lookCheck: Pausing, leaving the app or tab, or another interruption makes this a partial attempt. Save it separately and begin a fresh minute when ready.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to your own chord sound. This exercise counts completed changes rather than grading tone.

steps.title: Review, then optionally repeat
steps.action: Record the first attempt before another. If you choose a second trial, start from the other chord after resting and keep its result separate. Use 30 changes in a full minute as the early guide.
steps.lookCheck: Check the date, duration, starting chord, count, and whether you finished the full minute.
steps.listenCheck: Try the original study after the counting and beat-one lessons, and keep developing the sound of each chord.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You entered a count from several fragments.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Retain those as practice. For this checkpoint record one continuous 60-second attempt.
Save the count, slow down the anchor movement, and practice again. Use what you noticed to choose the next thing to work on.

practiceSegments.instruction: Recall the two shapes and prepare the first trial.
Optional second trial from the other starting chord; otherwise review slowly.
Record readiness and the next practice focus.

criteria: I recorded at least one actual, uninterrupted sixty-second trial.
My entered count uses the stated transition rule.
I recorded remembered shapes and basic position accuracy separately from the number.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Recall the A/D shapes and complete at least 30 changes in one full minute, counting each move yourself. Then try the study to use the changes in music.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Save the attempt for review and repeat the accuracy or anchor block that needs attention. You can keep learning while building your count.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own full-minute count and check of the remembered shapes.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: An automatic chord count, clear tone throughout, or playing a song. Sixty changes per minute is a later goal.

lessons.title: Four Beats, One Downstroke
lessons.objective: Read a four-beat bar and place one downstroke on beat 1 before adding more strokes.

steps.title: Find one complete bar
steps.action: Use the four-beat display at 60 BPM. Count 1, 2, 3, 4 aloud while tapping your knee. The next 1 begins a new bar; each number is one quarter-note beat.
steps.lookCheck: Four numbered beats make one bar. Count the separate lead-in before starting bar 1.
steps.listenCheck: Use an optional quiet click while learning, or follow the visual pulse.

steps.title: Sound only the first beat
steps.action: Hold D. On 1, make one downstroke across strings 4–1. Let it ring through 2, 3, 4 while continuing to count. Repeat without adding a second strike on the same 1.
steps.lookCheck: Read Downstroke on beat 1, then let the chord ring through beats 2, 3, and 4.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for one attack per bar, with time to prepare the next downstroke.

steps.title: Prepare the next chord
steps.action: Look at a D bar followed by an A bar. During the end of the D bar, prepare the change so the A downstroke belongs to the next 1. Slow down or rehearse the change separately if needed.
steps.lookCheck: The chord name tells what to hold; its bar and beat tell when to sound it.
steps.listenCheck: Keep counting evenly as you change. This is unscored practice.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You treat each beat as a new bar.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Trace all four beat cells before moving to the next bar number.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The chord change stops your count.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practice the count with knee taps, then the silent change, then combine them at a slower selected tempo.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read the bar and count-in labels.
Count four beats with knee taps at a comfortable pulse.
Sound one D downstroke on beat 1 of each bar, then try a D bar followed by A.
Explain the difference between one beat, one bar, and one downstroke.

criteria: I can count four beats per bar.
I can make one intended attack on beat 1 and let it ring.
I can identify where the next chord begins.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can follow the displayed bars at a manageable tempo and try the study's first phrase.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to count-and-tap practice, then add only one chord before changes.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own check of counting four beats and strumming on beat 1.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: A timing score, correct chord sound, or playing the complete study.

lessons.title: First Light: An Original A/D Study
lessons.objective: Rehearse and play a complete sixteen-bar original two-chord study with one downstroke per bar.

steps.title: Read the complete study
steps.action: Tune first. The study has 16 bars in 4/4 at a suggested 60 BPM. Its four-bar phrases are D D A A | D A D D | A A D D | A A D D. A separate four-beat count-in comes first. Begin with one downstroke on beat 1 of every bar.
steps.lookCheck: Follow the 16 numbered bars and their chord names. First Light is an original study.
steps.listenCheck: Listen to the optional synthesized demo with the microphone off, then stop it before your own attempt.

steps.title: Rehearse one phrase
steps.action: Begin with bars 1–4. Count the lead-in, strum the displayed chord on each 1, and let it ring through 2–4. Repeat the phrase with a new one-bar count-in. Then rehearse bars 5–8, 9–12, and 13–16.
steps.lookCheck: A loop's start and end are visible; its count-in is outside the numbered study bars.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for the intended chord and any missed first beat yourself. Slow the chosen tempo if changes disturb the pulse.

steps.title: Play from bar 1 to bar 16
steps.action: Turn looping off. After the count-in, follow the full score and play through bar 16. Let the final D ring through that bar's fourth beat. At 60 BPM the music lasts 64 seconds; including the count-in it lasts 68 seconds.
steps.lookCheck: Keep going until bar 16 ends. You can use the suggested practice block for several takes and rests.
steps.listenCheck: If you lose your place, note the bar and practice that phrase before a fresh full take.

steps.title: Record the musical attempt
steps.action: Mark whether you attempted all 16 bars, where you hesitated, and whether you used the guide or an external familiar-song lesson. When one stroke per bar feels comfortable, the optional four-downstrokes version uses one attack on each beat with the same chord sequence.
steps.lookCheck: The optional version contains 64 downstrokes; the starting version contains 16. Both still contain 16 bars.
steps.listenCheck: Record what you played and heard yourself. The app does not check chord identity or clean tone in either version.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Check the selected pattern. Sixteen strikes, one per beat, are four bars; this study needs all 16 bar numbers. In the starting pattern each strike begins a new four-beat bar.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A phrase is difficult during the full run.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Select that four-bar phrase, lower the tempo, and repeat with a visible lead-in. Start a new full take when ready.

practiceSegments.instruction: Tune, read the four phrases, and choose the starting strum pattern.
Try complete runs, with rests or phrase review between them.
Record one full-attempt observation and a bar to revisit; optional familiar-song practice can continue separately.

criteria: I know this is an original study and chose which strum pattern to practice.
I attempted all 16 bars at my chosen tempo or recorded exactly where I stopped.
I recorded my own observations about chord sound and staying with the beat.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Try the complete study, follow its chord plan, and choose a useful point to review. Keep learning while you improve.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Loop the uncertain phrase and keep the previous attempt visible. Use a slower tempo or one downstroke per bar.
selfAssessment.proves: Your record of practicing or attempting the complete original study.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Playing a familiar song, automatically checked chords, or a scored sixteen-bar timing check.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Sixteen Bars at Eighty
lessons.objective: Play sixty-four quarter-note downstrums across sixteen bars and review how closely you followed the beat.

steps.title: Prepare the complete timing check
steps.action: Choose a comfortable single chord or lightly muted strings. The full checkpoint is 16 bars of 4/4 at 80 BPM, with one downstroke on every beat. Rehearse more slowly first if needed. Stop reference sounds and backing audio before the microphone check.
steps.lookCheck: Count four beats in each of sixteen bars: 64 downstrokes altogether.
steps.listenCheck: The microphone checks when you strum. It cannot identify A, D, or whether a chord is correct.

steps.title: Follow all sixteen bars
steps.action: After a separate four-beat visual count-in, play beats 1–4 of each numbered bar from 1 through 16. Keep following the visual pulse until bar 16, beat 4 has sounded and the final bar ends.
steps.lookCheck: Follow beats 1–4 through all sixteen bars. At 80 BPM, each bar lasts 3 seconds; the music lasts 48 seconds plus a 3-second count-in.
steps.listenCheck: Count aloud in unscored practice if it helps. During the microphone check, follow the visual beats quietly so your voice is not mistaken for a strum.

steps.title: Interpret score and tempo separately
steps.action: Play through all 16 bars at 80 BPM or faster and earn a timing score of at least 75 to complete this checkpoint. Keep slower attempts as practice at the tempo you played.
steps.lookCheck: Read your BPM, matched strums out of 64, and timing score. A score of 75 describes timing; it is not a percentage of correct chords.
steps.listenCheck: If there is no reliable score, check the microphone and quiet the room, then try again. Check chord sound separately by ear.

steps.title: Compare the two strumming patterns
steps.action: This checkpoint has 64 strums over 16 bars. The study starts with 16 strums over the same number of bars because you play only on each 1. Keep your study notes, change counts, and timing results separate.
steps.lookCheck: The last downstroke is bar 16, beat 4. Keep going after the first 16 strums; those complete only four bars.
steps.listenCheck: Review uncertain timing separately from chord sound, then make a fresh complete sixteen-bar attempt.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: That completes four bars at one stroke per beat. Follow bars 1–16 and play all 64 beats.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The result includes sounds you did not intend as strums.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop reference and backing sounds, quiet the room, and try again. Other sharp sounds can be mistaken for strums.

mistakeRecovery.observation: You earned a timing score of at least 75 at a slower tempo.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep that result at the tempo you played. Increase the speed when ready; this checkpoint needs an 80-BPM or faster attempt.

practiceSegments.instruction: Prepare the quiet timing setup and inspect all sixteen bars.
Rehearse the quarter-note pulse without saving a score.
Make fresh complete timing attempts, leaving time to reset.
Review the tempo, timing score, and what you heard; choose what to revisit.

criteria: I played through sixteen bars with one downstroke on each of the 64 beats.
I checked my tempo, matched strums, and timing score.
I kept my timing result separate from chord checks, study notes, and change counts.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Play through all sixteen bars, with 64 downstrokes, at 80 BPM or faster and earn a timing score of at least 75.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Rehearse a shorter section or choose a slower tempo, then try a fresh full sixteen-bar run. If the microphone reading is unreliable, save your own practice notes and try the scored check later.
selfAssessment.proves: Any available timing score for this sixteen-bar attempt, at the tempo played.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Chord identity, clean tone, or a flawless performance. The score measures how closely your strums follow the beat.

lessons.title: A Riff Is a Melody You Can Hold
lessons.sourceTitle: A Riff Is a Melody You Can Hold
lessons.objective: Read and prepare Low E Lantern, an original eight-note riff that uses four positions on string 6.

steps.title: Read the one-string map
steps.action: Tune first. Low E Lantern stays on thick string 6. Read one fret number per beat: 0 2 3 2 | 0 2 5 3. Zero means play the open string; the other numbers name frets, not fingers.
steps.lookCheck: Keep your attention on string 6 and trace all eight numbers from left to right before playing.
steps.listenCheck: The four pitches are E2, F#2, G2, and A2. The repeated F#2 is a new pluck each time, not one held note.

steps.title: Prepare four positions
steps.action: Play open string 6, then fret 2 close to its body-side fret wire, fret 3, and fret 5. Use a comfortable fingering such as index at 2, middle at 3, and little finger at 5, or release and shift if the stretch creates tension.
steps.lookCheck: Your fingertip lands on string 6 without touching string 5. Keep the thumb and wrist comfortable rather than forcing a fixed shape.
steps.listenCheck: Play each position separately. Listen for the pitch to speak, then check buzz or an accidental second string yourself.

steps.title: Find the two-bar shape
steps.action: Tap eight even beats while saying 0, 2, 3, 2 | 0, 2, 5, 3. Then play only the first four notes. Rest, play only the second four, and finally join them at a pace you can control.
steps.lookCheck: The bar line divides two groups of four; it does not add a pause or an extra beat.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the first group return toward the open note, then hear the second group climb to fret 5 before ending on fret 3.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A fret number is being treated as a finger number.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Point to the numbered fret space first, then choose the comfortable finger that reaches it without strain.
Reduce the picking motion and aim through string 6 only. Stop, reset, and make one deliberate pluck.

practiceSegments.instruction: Read the eight fret numbers and name the four pitches.
Find open, fret 2, fret 3, and fret 5 separately on string 6.
Tap and say both four-note groups, then play each group slowly.
Join the two groups once and record what needs attention.

criteria: I can identify string 6 and all four fret positions.
I can explain that the tab numbers name frets, not fingers.
I tried both four-note groups without forcing a stretch.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can read the eight-note pattern and find all four positions at a comfortable pace with the tab visible.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Practice only 0–2–3–2, then only 0–2–5–3. Shift instead of stretching if fret 5 creates tension.
selfAssessment.proves: Your own reading and position check for the original one-string riff.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Measured pitch, timing, clean tone, memorization, or a completed performance.

lessons.title: One String, Four Notes
lessons.objective: Play the complete eight-note Low E Lantern riff on string 6 and use the coach to check the authored pitch order.

steps.title: Tune and isolate string 6
steps.action: Confirm standard tuning, then play only thick string 6. Review 0 2 3 2 | 0 2 5 3 and stop any reference sound before the microphone listens.
steps.lookCheck: The target card names string 6, its fret, and the expected pitch for every note.
steps.listenCheck: Check for one note at a time. The coach can recognize pitch, but only you can notice buzz or an adjacent string.

steps.title: Practice each half
steps.action: Choose Practice and loop targets 1–4 until 0–2–3–2 feels clear. Then loop targets 5–8 for 0–2–5–3. Practice waits for the requested pitch and does not save a score.
steps.lookCheck: Each target advances only after a fresh matching note; repeated pitches need another pluck or a brief mute.
steps.listenCheck: Use Pause and hear this note when needed. Let the synthesized reference finish before resuming.

steps.title: Join all eight notes
steps.action: Turn the loop off and rehearse the full riff. Start below 60 BPM if needed, keep one note per displayed slot, and raise the tempo only when the movement stays comfortable.
steps.lookCheck: Follow targets 1 through 8 without skipping. The bar line falls between targets 4 and 5.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for each fresh attack and for the final G2 to sound intentionally rather than as a stopped A2.

steps.title: Make a complete Play attempt
steps.action: Choose Play for the whole eight-note riff. A score of at least 75 at the selected tempo completes this exercise; slower attempts remain labeled with the BPM you actually used.
steps.lookCheck: Review matched pitches out of 8 and the saved BPM. Pitch-sequence mode checks the requested pitch inside each slot, not exact attack offset.
steps.listenCheck: After the result, separately note any buzz, extra strings, or tension that the microphone cannot judge.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The coach stays on a repeated F#2.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Release the ringing note with a brief mute or make a clear fresh pluck; one sustained pitch cannot fill two targets.

mistakeRecovery.observation: Fret 5 arrives late or feels strained.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Loop the second group more slowly. Release pressure and shift the hand toward fret 5 instead of forcing the little finger.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The room produces an unscored result.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Stop speaker audio, confirm the input, reduce background sound, and try again; an uncertain signal does not count as a failed performance.

practiceSegments.instruction: Tune and find all four positions with single deliberate notes.
Loop targets 1–4 and 5–8 separately in unscored Practice.
Join all eight notes at a comfortable selected tempo.
Make a complete Play attempt and review pitch evidence separately from tone.

criteria: I used string 6 and followed all eight fret positions in order.
I made a fresh pluck for every target, including repeated pitches.
I checked buzz, extra strings, and hand comfort myself.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete all eight slots in Play with at least a 75 pitch score at the tempo you chose, then review the separate tone self-check.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to one four-note loop, lower the tempo, or use the reference for one target before a fresh attempt.
selfAssessment.proves: The detected target-pitch order and actual BPM of a complete Play attempt.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Exact attack timing, physical string or finger choice, clean tone, relaxed technique, or memorization.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Three Complete Passes at Ninety
lessons.sourceTitle: Checkpoint: Three Clean Passes at Ninety
lessons.objective: Play three consecutive repeats of Low E Lantern at 90 BPM with every authored pitch detected in its assigned slot.

steps.title: Prepare one continuous checkpoint
steps.action: Tune, stop reference playback, and review the eight-note riff. The checkpoint is one 24-slot Play run: Low E Lantern three times without pausing or skipping, after a separate four-beat count-in.
steps.lookCheck: Targets 1–8 are pass 1, 9–16 are pass 2, and 17–24 are pass 3. Each pass keeps the same 0 2 3 2 | 0 2 5 3 order.
steps.listenCheck: Use unscored Practice first. During Play, keep reference sound off so it cannot become microphone evidence.

steps.title: Reach the authored tempo
steps.action: Build toward 90 BPM with the tempo control. Slower completed runs save their pitch score and actual BPM as rehearsal, but they do not complete this named checkpoint.
steps.lookCheck: The setup states both the selected BPM and the 90-BPM completion minimum.
steps.listenCheck: At 90 BPM, the 24 played slots last 16 seconds after the four-beat count-in.

steps.title: Fill every pitch slot
steps.action: In Play, make one fresh pluck for each displayed target. Completion requires a 100 pitch score at 90 BPM or faster, so all 24 authored slots must contain their requested pitch in one continuous run.
steps.lookCheck: Review matched pitches out of 24, score 100, and the actual BPM before continuing.
steps.listenCheck: A missing, different, or uncertain pitch prevents completion. Insufficient microphone evidence abstains instead of awarding a pass.

steps.title: Keep the claim honest
steps.action: Treat the saved result as pitch-in-slot evidence for three consecutive passes. The note cards remain visible, so this is not a memory test. Listen separately for buzz, accidental strings, unwanted ringing, and comfortable movement.
steps.lookCheck: The result reports pitch score, matched targets, target count, and BPM; it does not report clean tone or exact timing.
steps.listenCheck: If your self-check finds a tone or technique problem, keep the measured completion and choose that issue for the next practice block.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A slower run has all 24 pitches.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Keep the score as slower rehearsal and raise the tempo in small steps. Only a run at 90 BPM or faster completes this checkpoint.

mistakeRecovery.observation: One repeated note is not accepted.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Practice the boundary around that slot with a clear fresh pluck or brief mute, then start a new complete Play run.

mistakeRecovery.observation: The pitch result is complete but the sound was not clean to you.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: The app cannot certify tone. Rehearse the affected four-note group slowly and use your own listening check before the next run.

practiceSegments.instruction: Tune, review the tab, and stop all reference sound.
Rehearse one pass and build toward 90 BPM.
Practice joining pass 1 into pass 2 and pass 2 into pass 3.
Make fresh complete 24-slot Play attempts with rest between them.
Review pitch evidence, BPM, and the separate tone and comfort self-check.

criteria: I played one uninterrupted 24-slot run containing three full riff passes.
I reviewed all 24 matched pitches, the 100 pitch score, and the actual BPM.
I checked tone, accidental strings, and hand comfort separately by ear and feel.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete one continuous Play run with all 24 pitch slots detected at 90 BPM or faster, then make the separate tone and comfort self-check.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Keep the latest run at its real BPM, loop the uncertain four-note group in Practice, and make a fresh complete run when ready.
selfAssessment.proves: All 24 authored target pitches were detected in their assigned slots across three consecutive passes at the saved BPM.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Exact attack timing, clean tone, physical string or finger choice, memorization, relaxed technique, or a flawless performance.

lessons.title: Why Minor Sounds Like That
lessons.objective: Hear the minor third in Em, Am, and Dm, then place each open shape without squeezing.

steps.title: Compare E colors
steps.action: Play E major, then lift the index from string 3 fret 1 for E minor. Name the changed note.
steps.lookCheck: E major frets 3/1; E minor leaves string 3 open.
steps.listenCheck: The open G in Em sounds darker than G-sharp in E.

steps.title: Build E minor
steps.action: Place middle on string 5 fret 2 and ring on string 4 fret 2; strum all six strings.
steps.lookCheck: Both fingers arch over their strings and strings 3–1 stay open.
steps.listenCheck: Pluck strings 6–1 one at a time and find any buzz.

steps.title: Build A and D minor
steps.action: Am: mute 6, then 5 open, 4/3 fret 2, 2 fret 1, 1 open. Dm: mute 6/5, then 4 open, 3/2, 2/3, 1/1.
steps.lookCheck: Say Am uses strings 5–1 and Dm uses 4–1 before strumming.
steps.listenCheck: Hear A and D as separate bass homes, with the minor color above each.

steps.title: Use the color
steps.action: Strum Em, Am, Dm for four counts each, stopping between shapes to name the bass string.
steps.lookCheck: Use the same relaxed downstroke while only the shape changes.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for root changes and for open strings to ring.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Check that the minor third is open: string 3 in Em, string 2 fret 1 in Am, string 2 fret 3 in Dm.
Pluck that string alone, release excess pressure, and place the fingertip just behind its fret wire.
Place one finger at a time, move the thumb behind the neck, and pause rather than squeezing.

practiceSegments.instruction: Build Em, Am, and Dm string by string.
Cycle the three shapes for four counts.
Repeat and note one listening change.

criteria: I can state the sounding strings for Em, Am, and Dm.
I can identify the changed third in E.
I checked buzz and muting by ear.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can place the three shapes with sounding-string rules visible and explain the darker third.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use one shape at a time, pluck its fretted notes, then rebuild the chord.
selfAssessment.proves: Your shape and listening understanding of three open minor chords.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Chord speed, tone quality, intonation, or microphone evidence.

lessons.title: Three Minors on Cue
lessons.objective: Recall Em, Am, and Dm from spoken calls, then verify each permitted string deliberately.

steps.title: Shuffle the calls
steps.action: Say Em, Am, and Dm in a shuffled order and allow yourself five seconds to prepare each.
steps.lookCheck: Keep the card visible as a reading aid; this does not claim hidden memory.
steps.listenCheck: Name the lowest sounding string before strumming.

steps.title: Place from the bass
steps.action: Start Em on 6, Am on 5, and Dm on 4, then add the remaining fretted notes.
steps.lookCheck: Keep unused strings away from the pick path and fingers arched.
steps.listenCheck: Pluck the bass and each fretted note before a full chord.

steps.title: Run a two-pass check
steps.action: First pass forms the shape; second pass inspects bass, fretted notes, open strings, and omissions.
steps.lookCheck: A slow check is more useful than a rushed shape.
steps.listenCheck: A dead inner note means repeat the shape, not just strum louder.

steps.title: Add four-count changes
steps.action: At 60 BPM hold each called chord for four beats, changing on the next bar for six calls.
steps.lookCheck: The metronome marks the change point; it does not grade tone.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for the new root on beat 1 and reset silently if needed.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Say the name aloud, place its bass finger first, and restart calmly.
Compare bass strings 6, 5, and 4 by plucking them before the chord.
Use ten seconds for two rounds, then shorten only while the wrist stays relaxed.

practiceSegments.instruction: Shuffle and place six chord calls.
Run the bass and sounding-string check.
Change every four beats at 60 BPM.

criteria: I named the bass string for every call.
I checked permitted strings instead of only strumming.
I found one transition to revisit.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete six shuffled calls with correct sounding-string checks and no forced squeeze.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use only two shapes, give each ten seconds, and pluck its bass before strumming.
selfAssessment.proves: Manual recall and listening for three open minor shapes.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Three-second speed, tone, or automatic chord recognition.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Three Minors, Self-Checked
lessons.objective: Run a deliberate circuit of Em, Am, and Dm with manual string checks before moving to the next open-chord module.

steps.title: Prepare three calls
steps.action: Shuffle Em, Am, and Dm and keep their diagrams available for each call.
steps.lookCheck: This is a self-check of the three new minor shapes; it does not test hidden recall or three-second speed.
steps.listenCheck: Name the lowest permitted string first.

steps.title: Inspect each shape
steps.action: Pluck the bass and fretted strings before four even downstrokes.
steps.lookCheck: Em sounds 6–1; Am omits 6; Dm omits 6 and 5. Verify each minor diagram.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for dead inner notes hidden by a full strum.

steps.title: Run the circuit
steps.action: At 60 BPM hold each called minor for one four-count bar; silently reset when needed.
steps.lookCheck: Mark a call for review instead of hiding a scramble; the eight-shape circuit comes in the next module.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for the root on beat 1 and ringing open strings.

steps.title: Review honestly
steps.action: Repeat the weakest minor call for three slow bars and write the issue you heard.
steps.lookCheck: There is no app measurement attached to this checkpoint.
steps.listenCheck: Separate buzz, omission, transition tension, and comfort in your notes.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Use the minor diagram and build from its bass with a full breath.

mistakeRecovery.observation: A dead note is hard to find.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Pluck upward one string at a time until the contact is identified.
Return to four-count bars with silent resets between calls.

practiceSegments.instruction: Review the Em, Am, and Dm diagrams.
Run six shuffled four-count calls across the three minors.
Repeat the weakest minor call string by string.

criteria: I checked permitted strings for Em, Am, and Dm.
I completed or documented a six-call circuit across the three minors.
I wrote two tone or comfort observations.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete the six-call minor circuit and document any shape needing review; this is a self-check.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use one minor at a time and pluck every unclear string before returning to the shuffled calls.
selfAssessment.proves: A manual check of Em, Am, and Dm.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Three-second recall, clean tone, or microphone evidence.

lessons.title: The Stretch Chords
lessons.objective: Build E, C, and G with low effort, using each shape's bass and omitted-string rules.

steps.title: Map the basses
steps.action: Say E, C, G while touching their lowest strings: 6, 5, 6.
steps.lookCheck: C's string 6 is silent; begin its check on string 5.
steps.listenCheck: Hear the root move E–C–G even as open notes overlap.

steps.title: Build E major
steps.action: Place index 3/1, middle 5/2, ring 4/2 and strum six strings.
steps.lookCheck: Strings 2 and 1 are open; keep fingertips arched.
steps.listenCheck: Pluck 6 through 1 and correct buzz before strumming.

steps.title: Reach C safely
steps.action: Place ring 5/3, middle 4/2, index 2/1; mute 6 and leave 3 and 1 open.
steps.lookCheck: Move the whole hand toward the nut instead of reaching one finger.
steps.listenCheck: The open G on string 3 must ring.

steps.title: Build G
steps.action: Place middle 6/3, index 5/2, ring 1/3; let 4–2 ring open.
steps.lookCheck: Check fretted outer strings and relaxed thumb.
steps.listenCheck: Hear low and high G frame the open notes.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Bring the thumb behind the neck, move the elbow forward, and shorten the block.
Angle the ring finger or touch string 6 lightly with the thumb, then pluck it alone.
Pluck each string from 6 to 1 and repair the first dead contact.

practiceSegments.instruction: Locate E, C, and G roots.
Build E and inspect all strings.

criteria: I can name each root string.
I built C without forcing my wrist.
I checked each shape string by string.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: You can place E, C, and G with the bass rules visible and no hand strain.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Practice C in ten-second placements, then add its bass and open-string check.
selfAssessment.proves: A placement and listening plan for three open shapes.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Stretch tolerance, tone, speed, or measured chord score.

lessons.title: Four-Corner Turnaround: An Original Study
lessons.objective: Play the original E–C–G–D four-bar study with counted changes and a calm reset plan.

steps.title: Read the map
steps.action: The original study is E | C | G | D, one chord per four-count bar. Say the map aloud.
steps.lookCheck: No commercial melody or recording is needed.
steps.listenCheck: Hear bass movement E–C–G–D.

steps.title: Rehearse pairs
steps.action: Play E–C for two bars, then G–D for two, checking permitted strings.
steps.lookCheck: C omits 6 and D omits 6/5; keep that picking path.
steps.listenCheck: A silent reset is cleaner than a rushed chord.

steps.title: Join four bars
steps.action: At 60 BPM play E | C | G | D twice and change on bar lines.
steps.lookCheck: Count 1–2–3–4; the metronome guides rather than scores.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for each root on beat 1 and ring through 2–4.

steps.title: Shape the next take
steps.action: Make one full take, then isolate one hard transition for three slow repetitions.
steps.lookCheck: Name the transition rather than labeling the whole take.
steps.listenCheck: Check buzz, extra strings, and tension by ear and feel.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Say the destination on beat 4 and re-enter on beat 1.

mistakeRecovery.observation: C or D includes a low string.
mistakeRecovery.recovery: Mute the excluded string and pluck the bass before rebuilding.
Loop C | G at 40 BPM, then add surrounding bars.

criteria: I counted four beats in every bar.
I checked C and D omissions.
I identified one transition to revisit.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Play two original study passes and record transition and tone observations.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Return to the hardest pair at 40 BPM with silent resets.
selfAssessment.proves: A self-guided E–C–G–D study.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Commercial-song coverage, mastery, timing, or microphone scoring.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: Eight Open Shapes, Self-Checked
lessons.objective: Complete an eight-shape circuit including E, C, and G, checking every permitted string manually.

steps.title: Choose a circuit
steps.action: Use E, C, G, D, Em, Am, Dm, and A in a shuffled order with one four-count bar each.
steps.lookCheck: This is a manual reflection, not an automated clean-chord score.
steps.listenCheck: Name each root string before the first stroke.

steps.title: Inspect hard shapes
steps.action: For C/Am omit 6; for D/Dm omit 6/5; pluck bass and fretted notes first.
steps.lookCheck: Release pressure between checks and compare the diagram.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for a dead inner string.

steps.title: Play and mark
steps.action: At 60 BPM strum four downstrokes per chord and mark any scrambled change for review.
steps.lookCheck: A silent reset is allowed and should be recorded honestly.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for roots on beat 1 and open strings through 4.

steps.title: Repair two calls
steps.action: Repeat the two least reliable shapes for three slow bars and write the issue.
steps.lookCheck: Keep string, tone, and comfort notes separate.
steps.listenCheck: Use your ear for buzz and muting, not loudness.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Split into two groups of four and revisit after a rest.
Pluck upward while holding the shape until the contact is found.
Drop to 40 BPM for placement, then restore four counts.

criteria: I checked lowest and omitted strings.
I completed or documented the eight-bar circuit.
I wrote separate tone and comfort observations.
selfAssessment.readyWhen: Complete the eight-bar manual circuit and its follow-up checks.
selfAssessment.ifNotReady: Use four shapes at a time and isolate unclear strings.
selfAssessment.proves: A self-checked circuit across eight open shapes.
selfAssessment.doesNotProve: Speed, tone, finger pressure, timing, or microphone evidence.

lessons.title: The Hand Never Stops
lessons.objective: Coordinate constant down-up motion and controlled ghost strokes while keeping the spoken subdivision even.

steps.title: Air-strum
steps.action: Make small wrist-led down-up motions while saying 1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and.
steps.lookCheck: Down and up travel the same distance; elbow stays quiet.
steps.listenCheck: The spoken subdivisions remain even without guitar sound.

steps.title: Mute lightly
steps.action: Lay the fretting hand across strings and brush down-up at 50 BPM.
steps.lookCheck: Mute without pressing; pick crosses a narrow path.
steps.listenCheck: Hear a soft percussive tick on every subdivision.

steps.title: Miss on purpose
steps.action: Keep moving but lift above the strings on each upstroke, returning on the next down.
steps.lookCheck: Ghost timing stays; only contact changes.
steps.listenCheck: Hear a gap while the count continues.

steps.title: Transfer to Em
steps.action: Play two bars Em normally, then ghost every upstroke for two bars.
steps.lookCheck: Chord hand stays still while contact changes.
steps.listenCheck: Listen for equal spacing between pitched and muted strokes.

mistakeRecovery.recovery: Air-strum one bar while counting, then return to muted strings.
Shrink the wrist motion and shake out every four bars.
Raise the pick slightly and lighten contact.
